n: Asaph calls on God as the Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph’s tribes like a flock and sits enthroned above the cherubim on the ark. “Shine forth” — show yourself!

f.g: Enthroned above the winged cherubim on the ark’s lid.

n: Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh were the tribes of Rachel — Joseph and Benjamin’s families — who camped around the ark. The psalm likely reflects the northern kingdom’s crisis under Assyria.
The refrain (repeated in verses 7 and 19, growing stronger each time): restore us, let your face shine, and we will be saved.
Lord God of armies, how long will you be angry even when your people pray?

f.w: how long wilt thou be angry
f.g: Literally “how long will you smoke” — fuming anger.

n: Tears have become their daily bread and drink — sorrow in heaping portions.

f.g: By the bowlful; literally “a third” — a large measure.

n: Israel has become something neighbors fight over, and enemies laugh at them.
The refrain returns, now addressing the “God of hosts.”
An extended parable: Israel is a vine God brought out of Egypt and replanted in Canaan after clearing out the nations.

f.w: Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt

n: God cleared the ground, and the vine took deep root and filled the land.
It grew so large its shade covered the hills and its branches were like mighty cedars.

f.g: Literally “cedars of God” — the mightiest cedars.

n: Its branches reached to the Mediterranean Sea and its shoots to the Euphrates River — the full extent of David and Solomon’s kingdom.
Then why have you torn down its protective walls so every passerby can pick its fruit?

f.g: Stone walls or thorn hedges that protected a vineyard.

n: Wild boars ravage it and wild creatures feed on it — invading armies devouring the land.

f.w: The boar out of the wood
f.g: A wild boar — destructive in vineyards.

n: Turn back, God of armies! Look down from heaven and tend this vine again.
Care for the vine your own hand planted, the son you made strong for yourself.
It has been burned and cut down; its people perish under God’s rebuke.

May God’s hand rest on the man at his right hand, the son of man he strengthened. Originally this likely meant Israel or its king; Christians also hear a hint of Christ, the Son of Man at God’s right hand.

f.w: the man of thy right hand
f.g: A wordplay on Benjamin, whose name means “son of the right hand.”

n: Then we will never turn away from you again; give us life, and we will call on your name.
The refrain reaches its fullest form, using God’s covenant name: LORD God of hosts, restore us; shine on us, and we will be saved.
